title: Train/Validation/Test & Cross-validation
interviewAnswer: Use training data to fit parameters, validation data to make modeling choices, and test data only for final unbiased evaluation. Cross-validation estimates performance more robustly when data is limited.
why: Validation strategy determines whether offline metrics are believable. Many real ML failures come from a wrong split rather than a weak model.
intuition: Training data teaches the model. Validation data helps you choose the model. Test data estimates how the final chosen system generalizes. Cross-validation rotates the validation role across folds when data is limited.
deepDive: Random K-fold CV assumes samples are exchangeable. Stratification preserves class proportions; grouped splits keep related entities together; time-series splits preserve chronology. Any preprocessing learned from data—scaling, imputation, feature selection—must be fit inside each training fold, ideally using a Pipeline. Nested CV separates hyperparameter search from performance estimation when unbiased model-selection estimates matter.
math: K-fold estimate ≈ (1/K) Σ_k metric(model trained on all folds except k, evaluated on fold k)
workedExample: If ten slices come from the same patient or 3D volume, randomly splitting slices leaks near-duplicates across train and validation. Split by patient/volume instead.
code:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
for tr,va in cv.split(X,y,groups=patient_id):
    ...
commonMistakes: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set.
Fitting scaling or imputation on the full dataset before splitting.
Using random CV for future forecasting or grouped entities.
followUps: When would you use stratified CV?
production: Match offline splits to how the model will face new data in production: future time, unseen customers, unseen devices, or unseen sites. A realistic split is more valuable than a prettier metric.

visual.title: K-fold cross-validation
visual.caption: Each fold becomes validation once while the others train; time-series and grouped data require specialized splitting.
